title: A Blue Hour for the Glasshouse
premise: Silas Eastwick, a piano tuner who reads a building's past through its pipes and radiators, has spent fifteen years hiding inside the Glasshouse, the crumbling conservatory-estate they inherited but refuse to claim. When a late-night radio broadcast airs an unrecorded song Silas wrote as a teenager for their missing sister, Wren, it becomes proof that someone from the old household is alive and reaching out. Returning to the coastal town where their adoptive father's benevolence curdled into control, Silas must confront the family friend who took everything and decide whether claiming the house means becoming him. In the end, Silas signs the deed over to the found family of former wards who gather there, choosing kinship over ownership.
about_author: Mara Almeida is a former architectural conservator who spent a decade restoring historic houses along the Atlantic coast before turning to fiction full-time. Her work explores how buildings remember what people try to forget.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Key
chapters.summary: POV: Silas. Silas tunes pianos across the city by day and returns each night to the Glasshouse, which they maintain like a caretaker while insisting to themselves they are merely renting. Through radiator hums and floorboard creaks, we learn the house holds the memory of a family that dissolved fifteen years ago. The emotional beat is quiet avoidance — Silas keeps every room locked except two. Then, in a diner booth at midnight, the radio plays a song only one person alive could know.

chapters.title: What the Pipes Remember
chapters.summary: POV: Silas, with flashbacks in Wren's voice. Tracing the broadcast to a small coastal station, Silas learns the song was submitted anonymously with a return address near Harrow Point — where their adoptive father, Aldous Vane, ran his 'school' for gifted orphans. Flashbacks reveal Aldous's warmth rotting into surveillance and favoritism, and Wren's disappearance the night she tried to leave. The beat is dread sharpening into resolve: Silas packs a tuning kit and drives back toward the place they swore off.

chapters.title: A Blue Hour for the Glasshouse
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Silas and Merritt, another former ward now the town's postmistress. At Harrow Point, Silas finds the original Glasshouse — the estate was a copy all along — and discovers Merritt has been secretly broadcasting Wren's compositions to lure surviving wards home. But Aldous, dying and unrepentant, still holds Wren's letters hostage behind a legal claim on both houses. The climax comes at blue hour when Silas confronts him, using what the pipes taught them about listening to break his hold over the room.

chapters.title: Deed of Hands
chapters.summary: POV: Silas, closing in Merritt's voice. Wren is found — alive, changed, unwilling to be rescued but willing to be met. Silas tears up Aldous's claim, then does the unthinkable: transfers the deed to a trust held jointly by the surviving wards, dissolving their own power over the place that once imprisoned them. The final scene is the first true dinner in either Glasshouse, radiators singing. The beat is release — identity rebuilt not through inheritance but through chosen belonging.
